about: The 142 elements: one record each, with its place on the grid, theme, year, definition, talk question, hand-picked connections and benchmark area.

elements.name: Artificial Intelligence
elements.def: Computer systems, built and used by people, that do tasks we once thought only humans could do, such as translating text, recognising faces in photos or recommending what to watch next.
elements.talk: Name three things you used today that might have AI inside. How could you tell?
elements.picture_alt: An AI chip linked to three cards showing jobs that usually need a human mind: understanding words, spotting patterns and making choices.

elements.name: Latent Space
elements.def: The space of numbers inside a model where each input is placed as a point, so similar things, such as ‘cat’ and ‘kitten’, end up close together. Each point is an embedding (Em).
elements.talk: If an AI stores ideas as a map of numbers, can we ever be sure what it “thinks”?
elements.picture_alt: On a simplified map of word embeddings, kitten lands near cat and dog. Bus and train sit together in a different part of the map.

elements.name: Recursive Self-Improvement
elements.def: AI helping to build better AI, which could then build better AI still. The idea dates from 1965; today, AI companies already use their own models to help train and test the next ones.
elements.talk: If AI helps to build the next AI, who should check each new version before it is used?
elements.picture_alt: Three AI robots stand on rising steps, each one building a bigger next version, while a person below asks who checks them.

elements.name: Superintelligence
elements.def: A hypothetical AI that would far surpass the best human minds in almost every field. Experts disagree on whether, or when, it could arrive.
elements.talk: If an AI became cleverer than every person, who should decide what it is allowed to do?
elements.picture_alt: A bar chart for maths, science and art where a dashed, hypothetical super AI bar marked with a question mark towers over the best human.

elements.name: Artificial General Intelligence
elements.def: A hypothetical AI able to match or exceed human ability across almost any intellectual task, rather than excelling in one narrow domain.
elements.talk: How would we know if artificial general intelligence had arrived? Who should decide?
elements.picture_alt: A narrow AI that can do one of six tasks beside a dashed, hypothetical general AI that can do almost all of them.

elements.name: Machine Learning
elements.def: A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
elements.talk: How would you teach a computer to tell cats from dogs without describing either?
elements.picture_alt: Hand-written rules are crossed out; instead an AI learns from example pictures of cats and dogs, then recognises a new picture as a cat.

elements.name: Deep Learning
elements.def: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers — the approach behind most modern breakthroughs in vision, speech and language.
elements.talk: Deep learning needs huge amounts of data. Whose data should it be allowed to learn from?
elements.picture_alt: A picture passes through many stacked layers that find edges, then shapes, then parts, until the last layer says cat.

elements.name: Neural Network
elements.def: A model made of layers of connected nodes, loosely inspired by the brain, that learns by adjusting the strength of its connections.
elements.talk: In what ways is a neural network like a brain, and in what ways is it nothing like one?
elements.picture_alt: Input, hidden and output nodes in three layers, joined by thick strong connections and thin weak ones.

elements.name: Algorithm
elements.def: A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem; in machine learning, the method a system uses to learn from data.
elements.talk: Write an algorithm for making a cup of tea. What would a computer get wrong if one step were missing?
elements.picture_alt: Five numbered steps for making tea, from boiling the kettle to taking the bag out, ending at a steaming mug.
elements.year_note: The word comes from the 9th-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi; its machine-learning sense ("learning algorithm") dates from the late 1950s (Samuel, Rosenblatt).

elements.name: Model
elements.def: What you get after an algorithm has learned from data: the trained program that turns an input, such as a question or a photo, into an output.
elements.talk: Two models trained on different data are asked the same question. Should they give the same answer?
elements.picture_alt: A model built from data turns a photo into the answer dog, and the question three times four into twelve.

elements.name: Training
elements.def: The process of feeding data to a model and adjusting its internal settings until its outputs improve.
elements.talk: What might an AI get wrong if it only learned from photos taken in one country?
elements.picture_alt: Data goes in and the model guesses, the guess is checked, its settings are adjusted, and its score rises round by round.

elements.name: Inference
elements.def: Using a trained model to make predictions or generate output on new inputs — the “running” phase after training.
elements.talk: Every answer an AI gives uses energy. Does that change how often you would use it?
elements.picture_alt: After training, a model labels a new photo as a bird with 92% confidence. The prediction can still be wrong.
elements.year_note: This meaning (running a trained model on new inputs, as opposed to training it) became common with deep learning in the 2010s. Around 1970 "inference" in AI mostly meant logical inference, as in the "inference engines" of rule-based expert systems.
elements.teacher_note: Training a large model uses a lot of energy in one go; inference uses a little for each answer, which adds up across millions of uses. The "92%" is the model's own confidence, not a chance of being right: a model can be confidently wrong. Watch out later: in statistics, "inference" means almost the opposite, using data to work out a model's settings, which is closer to what AI calls training.

elements.name: Parameters
elements.def: The millions, billions or even trillions of numbers inside a model that it adjusts as it learns, like dials being tuned. A model’s size is often quoted in parameters.
elements.talk: Is a bigger model with more parameters always better? What else matters?
elements.picture_alt: A panel of twelve number dials inside a model, with one being turned from 0.42 to 0.47, and a note that there are billions more.

elements.name: Token
elements.def: The small chunk of text — a word, part of a word or a symbol — that language models read and write.
elements.talk: Why might AI find it hard to count the letters in a word it reads as tokens?
elements.picture_alt: The word "unbelievable" is cut into three tokens, un, believ and able, each with the number the model reads.

elements.name: Embedding
elements.def: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of text, images or other data, so that similar things sit close together.
elements.talk: If words are stored as numbers, which words do you think would sit close together? Why?
elements.picture_alt: A map of words: cat, kitten and dog sit close together, bus, car and train sit together far away, and each word is stored as a list of numbers.

elements.name: Transformer
elements.def: The design behind today’s large language models, introduced in 2017. Its “attention” lets it weigh up how each word in a passage relates to every other word.
elements.talk: Why might one invention in 2017 have changed so much about the AI we use today?
elements.picture_alt: Attention lines link the word it's to every word in the sentence 'The cat sleeps because it's tired', with the thickest line going to cat.

elements.name: Foundation Model
elements.def: A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many different tasks, rather than built for just one.
elements.talk: If many apps are built on the same few models, what happens when one of those models gets something wrong?
elements.picture_alt: Four apps for chat, tutoring, code and search are built on one large foundation model trained on broad data such as books, pictures and code.

elements.name: Large Language Model
elements.def: An AI model trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word (token), which lets it generate replies, summaries and translations – the kind of model behind most chatbots.
elements.talk: If a model only predicts the next word, can it understand what it writes? Argue both sides.
elements.picture_alt: A pile of books labelled billions of words feeds a language model, which guesses the next word in 'The cat sat on the…', with 'mat' far more likely than 'sofa' or 'moon'.

elements.name: Generative AI
elements.def: AI that creates new content — text, images, audio, video or code — rather than only analysing existing data.
elements.talk: What have you seen this week that might have been made by generative AI?
elements.picture_alt: An AI sends arrows out to five new things it has made: text, an image, audio, a video and code.

elements.name: Prompt
elements.def: The instruction or input you give a generative model to get a response.
elements.talk: Turn "help with my homework" into a clear prompt. What did you add?
elements.picture_alt: A chat box marked prompt reads 'Write a 3-line poem about rain for Year 7', and an AI answers with a poem beginning 'Drip, drop, rain on the roof'.

elements.name: Prompt Engineering
elements.def: The craft of writing and structuring prompts to get more accurate, useful and consistent outputs.
elements.talk: Write the same request three ways. Which prompt gets the most useful answer, and why?
elements.picture_alt: The broad prompt “Help with fractions” becomes “Show three quarters using four equal tiles.” The answer shows three shaded tiles and one empty tile.

elements.name: Context Window
elements.def: The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can take into account at once.
elements.talk: What happens in a very long chat when the AI starts to forget what you said at the start?
elements.picture_alt: A frame encloses the recent chat messages available for this response. Earlier messages sit outside the current context window.

elements.name: Multimodal AI
elements.def: A model that can take in or produce more than one type of data, such as text, images and audio together.
elements.talk: An AI that can see, hear and read at once: what could it help with, and what new risks does it bring?
elements.picture_alt: A picture of a bird, the question 'What bird?' and a sound wave all go into one AI, which answers 'A robin, singing'.

elements.name: Diffusion Model
elements.def: A generative model trained on pictures that have had random speckles (‘noise’) added, so it learns to remove the noise. To make a new picture, it starts from pure noise and cleans it up step by step.
elements.talk: An AI makes a picture from noise. Is the picture original? Who is the artist?
elements.picture_alt: Three small squares go from pure noise to a clearer and clearer picture, step by step, ending in a new picture of hills and a sun.

elements.name: Generative Adversarial Network
elements.def: Two networks in competition — one generates content, the other judges it — until the output looks realistic.
elements.talk: Two AIs compete until a fake looks real. How could this be used for good, and for harm?
elements.picture_alt: A maker AI hands a drawn flower to a judge AI with a magnifying glass, who says 'Fake!', and a dashed arrow sends the maker back to try again.

elements.name: Text-to-Image
elements.def: AI that makes a picture from a written description, such as ‘a fox reading a book in a library, cartoon style’. The tool fills in many details you did not ask for.
elements.talk: With your teacher, using a school-approved tool, make an image, then list every decision the AI made that you did not ask for.

elements.name: Text-to-Speech
elements.def: Converting written text into natural-sounding synthetic speech.
elements.talk: If an AI can speak in any voice, how could you be sure a voice note is really from a friend?
elements.picture_alt: The typed words 'Hi, class!' turn into a playing sound wave, and a speaker plays a natural voice to a listener.

elements.name: Fine-Tuning
elements.def: Taking a model that has already been trained on lots of general data and training it a bit more on a smaller set of examples, such as medical notes, so it does better at one job.
elements.talk: If you could train an AI to be an expert in one subject, which would you choose and what would it need to learn from?
elements.picture_alt: A general model, trained more on a small stack of maths data, becomes a maths expert.

elements.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
elements.def: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): a system first looks up relevant documents, such as a school’s policies, and gives them to the model so its answer can draw on them. The answer can still be wrong.
elements.talk: Does looking things up first make an AI answer trustworthy? What if the source is wrong?
elements.picture_alt: A question, "When is sports day?", goes to a stack of documents. The AI finds the right one in the calendar and answers "Friday 4 July", marked with its source.

elements.name: Temperature
elements.def: A setting that controls randomness in output: low is focused and predictable, high is varied and creative.
elements.talk: Would you want a high or a low temperature for a story, a revision quiz and a medical answer?
elements.picture_alt: A thermometer next to the prompt 'My pet is a…': at high temperature the answers are varied, 'dragon, cloud, toaster'; at low they are predictable, 'dog, dog, dog'.

elements.name: Chain-of-Thought
elements.def: Asking a model to write out steps before its final answer, which often improves results. The written steps may not show how the answer was really produced. Compare Reasoning Model (Rm).
elements.talk: Does an AI showing its working make the answer more trustworthy? How would you check?
elements.picture_alt: A word problem about packs of pens is worked through in three numbered steps, including a check, before the final answer of 14 pens.

elements.name: Few-Shot Learning
elements.def: Showing a model a handful of examples in the prompt so it can pick up a new task without retraining.
elements.talk: Give an AI three examples and it copies the pattern. How is that like learning from a worked example?
elements.picture_alt: Three examples, dog to woof, cow to moo and sheep to baa, are followed by a new one, duck, which the AI correctly completes as quack.

elements.name: Reasoning Model
elements.def: A model trained to spend extra computation “thinking” through a problem before answering, improving maths, coding and logic.
elements.talk: With your teacher, using a school-approved tool, ask an AI to show its working on a maths problem. Check every step: is each one right?
elements.picture_alt: An AI thinks for 20 seconds about x + 5 = 12, crosses out a wrong try, checks the right one, then answers x = 7.

elements.name: Synthetic Data
elements.def: Artificially generated data used to train or test models when real data is scarce, sensitive or expensive.
elements.talk: When is it fair to train AI on made-up data, and when could it hide real problems?
elements.picture_alt: A few locked real records go into a machine that makes look-alikes, and the many made-up records are used to train an AI.

elements.name: Hallucination
elements.def: When an AI produces confident-sounding information that is false or made up, such as a book that does not exist. It happens mainly because the model predicts likely-sounding words rather than checking facts.
elements.talk: With your teacher, using a school-approved tool, ask an AI for three sources on a topic. Do they all exist, and do they say what it claims?
elements.picture_alt: A chatbot says "Smith (2019) proves it! 100% sure", but the journal article it cites is only a dashed outline stamped "Not real".

elements.name: Deepfake
elements.def: Realistic AI-made or edited video, audio or images showing people saying or doing things they never did. Sexual fakes of under-18s are illegal; if you see one, tell a trusted adult or use Childline’s Report Remove.
elements.picture_alt: In the original recording, a coach says kick-off is at ten. An AI imitation sounds like the coach announcing the match is off, words the coach never said.
elements.talk: How would you check whether a shocking video of a famous person is real?
elements.teacher_note: Any sexual image of someone under 18, including an AI-made fake, is illegal to make, keep or share. In England and Wales it is also an offence to make, or ask someone to make, a sexual deepfake of an adult without their consent (Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 138, in force since 6 February 2026).

elements.name: Vibe Coding
elements.def: Building software by describing what you want in plain language and accepting the code an AI tool writes, often without reading or checking it closely.
elements.talk: If AI writes code that breaks something, whose job is it to fix it?
elements.picture_alt: A person asks for a quiz with a timer, the AI writes the code, and the finished quiz app runs.

elements.name: Context Engineering
elements.def: Structuring everything you give an AI, including background documents, rules and examples, rather than relying on a single clever prompt.
elements.talk: What background would you give an AI so it could help with your homework fairly?
elements.picture_alt: A box packed with documents, rules, examples and the task is passed to an AI, showing everything it needs rather than one prompt.

elements.name: Generative Video
elements.def: AI that creates video clips from a text description, an image or another video.
elements.talk: What clues might show that a video was generated? Are they reliable?

elements.name: AI Slop
elements.def: Low-effort, mass-produced AI text, images and videos that flood social media and search results.
elements.talk: Look at examples your teacher has chosen. How can you tell AI slop from something made with care?
elements.picture_alt: A phone feed is filled with the same low-effort picture posts saying Wow, numbered one after another, with thousands more spilling out and the scroll never ending.

elements.name: 2D Design
elements.def: Flat designs such as drawings, logos, layouts and laser-cut parts. AI tools can now suggest, generate and refine them.
elements.talk: If AI designs a logo for you in seconds, what is left for a human designer to do?
elements.picture_alt: A rough star sketch is turned by AI into three flat badge designs, and the person picks the shield one.

elements.name: 3D Design & CAD
elements.def: Designing objects in three dimensions with computer-aided design (CAD) software, ready to model, 3D print or manufacture. AI can generate and improve designs.
elements.talk: What would you design and 3D print if AI helped you? Who owns the design?
elements.picture_alt: A 3D CAD model of a 40 mm block with axes is made lighter by AI with a hole, then sent to a 3D printer building it layer by layer.

elements.name: Supervised Learning
elements.def: Training a model on labelled examples, where every input comes with the correct answer, such as thousands of photos each tagged ‘cat’ or ‘dog’.
elements.talk: If the labels a model learns from are wrong, what will the model learn?
elements.picture_alt: Two example cards, an apple labelled apple and a banana labelled banana, feed an AI, which then labels a new unlabelled apple as apple.

elements.name: Unsupervised Learning
elements.def: Training a model to find patterns or groups in data that has no labels, such as sorting songs by how similar they sound, without being given the right answers. Contrast with supervised learning.
elements.talk: If an AI groups people without being told how, how would you know whether the groups are fair?
elements.picture_alt: A jumbled pile of circles, triangles and squares with no labels is sorted by the AI into three groups of matching shapes.

elements.name: Regression
elements.def: Predicting a continuous number, such as a price, a demand level or a temperature.
elements.talk: Could you predict someone’s test score from how many hours they revised? What would the prediction miss about them?
elements.picture_alt: A scatter graph of hours revised against test score with a straight best-fit line, used to predict a score of 72 for 6 hours of revision.

elements.name: Classification
elements.def: Assigning inputs to categories, such as spam or not spam, fraudulent or genuine.
elements.talk: Sorting emails into spam and not spam sounds simple. What could go wrong, and who would it affect?
elements.picture_alt: Two emails, one saying 'You won £1000!' and one about maths homework, go through an AI that sorts them into a Spam bin and a Not spam bin.

elements.name: Clustering
elements.def: Grouping similar items together when no one has said in advance what the groups should be, such as a shop sorting customers by what they tend to buy.
elements.talk: Sort your class's favourite apps into groups. Would a computer choose the same groups? Why not?
elements.picture_alt: Shop customers plotted by visits and spend form three separate clusters, marked Group A, Group B and Group C.

elements.name: Decision Tree
elements.def: A model that makes predictions through a flowchart of yes/no questions about the data.
elements.talk: Draw a yes/no flowchart to decide what to wear. What does it get wrong about real people?
elements.picture_alt: A yes/no flowchart asks 'Raining?' then 'Cold?', and for a dry, cold day it ends at Jumper rather than Coat or T-shirt.

elements.name: Random Forest
elements.def: Many decision trees combined, whose collective vote gives a more robust prediction than any single tree.
elements.talk: Is asking a hundred decision trees and taking the vote like asking a crowd? When is a crowd wrong?
elements.picture_alt: Three small decision trees each vote, two saying yes and one saying no, and the combined vote gives Yes by 2 to 1.

elements.name: Gradient Boosting
elements.def: Building many small models one after another, each fixing the mistakes of the one before, so together they make good predictions from tables of data.
elements.talk: Each model in the chain is built to fix the errors of the one before. How is that similar to, and different from, a person learning from their mistakes?
elements.picture_alt: For a training example with a known price of £10, the starting estimate is £6. Successive models contribute £3 and £1. Each bar adds the new contribution to the running prediction.

elements.name: Feature Engineering
elements.def: Selecting and transforming raw data into inputs (features) that help a model predict well.
elements.talk: If you were predicting who enjoys a book, which facts about a reader would you use, and which would be unfair?
elements.picture_alt: Raw facts about a reader are turned into features: born 2012 becomes age 14, 36 books in 3 years becomes 12 books a year, and their name is left out.

elements.name: Overfitting
elements.def: When a model memorises its training data so closely that it performs poorly on new, unseen data.
elements.talk: A student memorises past papers but cannot answer a new question. How is that like overfitting?
elements.picture_alt: A wavy curve passes through every training point. The same curve misses four new observations, with dashed lines showing the prediction errors.

elements.name: Forecasting
elements.def: Predicting future values — sales, demand, traffic — from historical patterns.
elements.talk: What would you want an AI to forecast for your school, and what should it never predict about people?
elements.picture_alt: A bar chart of lunches sold each week, with solid bars for past weeks and dashed bars after 'Now' forecasting the coming weeks.

elements.name: Time Series
elements.def: Data recorded at regular times, such as daily temperatures or weekly attendance, and the methods for spotting its trends and repeating patterns.
elements.talk: What patterns can you spot in your school's attendance over a year? Would a computer spot the same ones?
elements.picture_alt: A line chart of ice creams sold over 2025 and 2026 that peaks every summer, with a dashed trend line showing sales going up overall.

elements.name: Anomaly Detection
elements.def: Spotting unusual data points or behaviour, such as fraud, equipment faults or security breaches.
elements.talk: Your bank blocks a payment that looks unusual. Is that helpful or annoying? Who decides what is unusual?
elements.picture_alt: A list of card payments of £4, £2 and £3, with one £950 payment made abroad at 3am highlighted and stamped unusual.

elements.name: Predictive Analytics
elements.def: Using historical data and statistical models to estimate what is likely to happen next.
elements.talk: Should a school use AI to predict which students might struggle? What could help, and what could harm?
elements.picture_alt: Lunch counts from past Fridays, 230, 245 and 238, feed into a model that estimates about 240 lunches next Friday.

elements.name: Prescriptive Analytics
elements.def: Going beyond predicting what will happen to recommending the best action to take.
elements.talk: If an AI recommends what you should do next, would you follow it? When would you ignore it?
elements.picture_alt: A forecast of rain at 2pm leads to three sports day plans, with starting at 10am marked as the best choice over going ahead at 2pm or cancelling.

elements.name: Recommendation Engine
elements.def: A system that suggests products, content or actions based on a person’s behaviour and preferences.
elements.talk: Why might your feed look completely different from your friend's?
elements.picture_alt: A person has watched two football clips and a music clip, and their feed now suggests more football.

elements.name: Churn Prediction
elements.def: Identifying which customers are likely to leave, so a business can act before they do.
elements.talk: A streaming app predicts you will cancel and offers a discount. Is that helpful or sneaky?
elements.picture_alt: Three streaming app subscribers are scored for their chance of leaving, 12%, 20% and 85%, and the one most likely to leave is sent a half-price offer.

elements.name: Sentiment Analysis
elements.def: Detecting the emotional tone — positive, negative or neutral — in text such as reviews or social posts.
elements.talk: Can a computer tell when someone is being sarcastic? Write a sarcastic sentence and discuss why a computer might misread it.
elements.picture_alt: An AI reads three reviews and tags 'Loved it, 10/10!' as positive, 'It was OK.' as neutral and 'Never again.' as negative.

elements.name: Natural Language Processing
elements.def: Natural language processing (NLP) is the field of AI that builds systems to process, analyse and produce human language, such as translation apps, spellcheckers and voice assistants.
elements.talk: Which languages and accents do voice assistants understand best? Who gets left out?
elements.picture_alt: A person says 'Set a timer for ten minutes' and the AI turns it into a task, start a timer, lasting 10 minutes.

elements.name: Computer Vision
elements.def: The field of AI that lets machines interpret images and video, from recognising faces to spotting defects on a production line.
elements.talk: Who should be told when a camera is recognising things, and how?
elements.picture_alt: A camera above a production line checks each bottle, marks three as OK and spots a crack in the fourth.

elements.name: Generative Engine Optimisation
elements.def: Writing and arranging web content so that AI chatbots and AI search answers are more likely to mention or link to it, like a business trying to appear first in Google results. Also called answer engine optimisation.
elements.talk: If companies shape what AI assistants recommend, how can you tell an answer is fair?
elements.picture_alt: Someone asks an AI assistant for the best bike lights, and its answer cites a web page written with clear questions and answers as its source.

elements.name: AI Agent
elements.def: A system that uses an AI model to pursue a goal by deciding on and taking actions, not just answering questions.
elements.talk: What should an AI agent always check with you before doing it on your behalf?
elements.picture_alt: A bot is given the goal 'Book the hall' and works through the steps itself, ticking off 'Check diary' and 'Email office', then pauses at 'Pay £50?' and asks a person first.

elements.name: Agentic AI
elements.def: AI that can plan, use tools and carry out several steps of a job by itself, with a person checking in only now and then.
elements.talk: Which jobs would you trust an AI to finish on its own, and which should always be checked?
elements.picture_alt: A bot travels along a winding path of numbered steps, Plan, Search, Draft and Send, to a 'Done' flag, with a person checking in only once along the way.

elements.name: Autonomy
elements.def: How much an AI system can decide and do on its own before a human needs to step in.
elements.talk: Should a self-driving bus, a marking tool and a chatbot each have the same amount of freedom? Why not?
elements.picture_alt: Three sliders run from 'Human decides' to 'AI alone': a spelling fix is set almost fully to the AI, homework marks halfway, and exam grades almost entirely to a human.

elements.name: Planning
elements.def: An agent breaking a goal down into ordered steps and deciding what to do next.
elements.talk: Plan a school trip in five steps. Which step would you trust an AI to plan, and which not?
elements.picture_alt: A bot stands at the bottom of four numbered steps, Date, Coach, Forms and Pack, that climb to a 'Trip day' flag, with the second step marked 'Next'.

elements.name: Memory
elements.def: How an AI tool stores information to use later, either during one task (short-term) or between separate conversations (long-term), such as a chatbot saving your name.
elements.talk: What do you think an AI tool remembers about you? How could an adult help you check?
elements.picture_alt: Three separate chats each have their own short-term note, while one long-term memory bar under all three keeps the fact 'Likes chess'.

elements.name: Function Calling
elements.def: A way for an AI model to ask other software, such as a calculator, a search engine or a booking system, to do a job; the app around the model runs the request. Also called tool use.
elements.talk: Which tools should an AI never be given access to, and why?
elements.picture_alt: Asked '17 × 23 = ?', a bot calls a calculator tool rather than search or booking, and the answer 391 comes back.

elements.name: ReAct
elements.def: A pattern where an agent alternates between reasoning about a problem and acting with tools (Reason + Act).
elements.talk: When you solve a problem, how often do you stop, plan and try again? How is an AI system that writes out a plan, uses a tool, then checks the result similar to you, and how is it different?
elements.picture_alt: An agent takes turns to think and act: 'Think: rain later?', 'Act: check weather', 'Think: rain at 3pm', 'Act: move the match', ending with a tick.

elements.name: Agent Loop
elements.def: The cycle an AI agent repeats (look at the situation, choose an action, act, check the result) until the goal is met or a person stops it.
elements.talk: An agent keeps trying until it succeeds. When should it stop and ask a person instead?
elements.picture_alt: A bot sits inside a loop of four steps, Observe, Think, Act and Check, that goes round again and again, with a way out to 'Done' from Check.

elements.name: Self-Reflection
elements.def: An agent reviewing and critiquing its own work, then correcting mistakes before it finishes.
elements.talk: Can an AI really check its own work? Who should check the checker?
elements.picture_alt: A bot looks back at its draft, circles the wrong answer in '7 × 8 = 54', and its final version reads '7 × 8 = 56' with a 'Checked' label.

elements.name: Model Context Protocol
elements.def: A shared set of rules (MCP) that lets AI assistants connect to other tools and data, such as a calendar or a folder of files, in the same way every time.
elements.talk: What could go well, and what could go wrong, if every AI tool could connect to your files in the same way?
elements.picture_alt: An AI helper plugs into a bar labelled MCP, which connects it to a calendar, files and email using the same plug for every tool.

elements.name: Agent-to-Agent (A2A)
elements.def: Shared rules that let AI agents made by different companies find each other and work together on a task.
elements.talk: If AI agents from different companies talk to each other, who is responsible when they make a mistake?
elements.picture_alt: Two AI agents from different makers, a school AI and a coach company AI, use shared A2A rules to agree a coach booking for 30 people on Friday.

elements.name: Orchestrator
elements.def: A part of an AI system that splits a big task into smaller jobs, hands them to other agents or tools, then puts their results together. Contrast with Workflow Orchestration, which plans a whole business process.
elements.talk: An AI manager hands out jobs to other AIs. What should a human manager still do?
elements.picture_alt: A lead agent is asked to plan a trip, hands out jobs on trains, the hotel and the weather to three helpers, then combines their answers into one trip plan.

elements.name: Multi-Agent System
elements.def: Several specialised agents working together, each handling one part of a larger task.
elements.talk: A team of AIs each does one part of a job. How is that like group work, and where could it go wrong?
elements.picture_alt: Three AI agents each do one part of making a quiz, one writing the questions, one drawing the picture and one checking the finished sheet.

elements.name: Agent Swarm
elements.def: A large group of simple agents coordinating to solve problems collectively, inspired by swarms in nature.
elements.talk: Ants, birds and bees work together without a leader. Should AI agents work that way too?
elements.picture_alt: A stream of many small, simple agents travels from a start point to a goal with no leader, each one copying the direction of its neighbours.

elements.name: Reinforcement Learning
elements.def: A way of training a program by trial and error: it gets a reward score for good actions and is adjusted to get more rewards. Chatbots are partly tuned this way, using people’s ratings of their answers.
elements.talk: How is learning by trial and reward like the way you learned a game? What is different?
elements.picture_alt: An agent tries routes through a maze, losing a point in a trap and winning ten points at a star, while its score rises over many tries and people rate chatbot answers plus one or minus one.

elements.name: Computer Use
elements.def: An AI agent that controls a computer by taking screenshots, moving the cursor and typing, so it can use ordinary apps the way a person would.
elements.talk: Would you let an AI use your computer for you? What would you never let it click?
elements.picture_alt: An AI agent reads what is on a computer screen, types a name into a box on the keyboard and moves the cursor to click Save.

elements.name: Browser Agent
elements.def: An agent that navigates websites, fills in forms and completes online tasks on your behalf.
elements.talk: If an AI books something online for you and gets it wrong, who should put it right?
elements.picture_alt: A person asks for two cinema seats, and an AI agent in the web browser fills in the seats and day on the booking form and clicks Book.

elements.name: Coding Agent
elements.def: An AI agent that writes, tests and fixes code across a whole project, with a programmer setting the task and checking the changes before they are used.
elements.talk: If AI writes the code, which coding skills should people still learn?
elements.picture_alt: An AI agent works across several code files in a repeating loop of write, test and fix until the result shows 12 tests pass.

elements.name: Robotic Process Automation
elements.def: Software ‘bots’ that copy the clicks and typing a person would do, to repeat the same fixed steps, such as copying data from emails into a spreadsheet (RPA).
elements.talk: Which boring, repetitive task at school would you hand to a bot? What could go wrong?
elements.picture_alt: A software bot copies a name from a list into a form and clicks Submit, repeating the same steps 500 times.

elements.name: Intelligent Automation
elements.def: Combining simple software bots with AI tools that can pull out information and pick between options, so computers can handle jobs that are not just fixed rules, like sorting emails by topic.
elements.talk: Pick a job a person does at school, such as marking or answering the office phone. What would we gain and lose if a machine did it?
elements.picture_alt: AI reads a parent's email saying Sam is ill, decides it is an absence, and a bot marks Sam as ill in the register.

elements.name: Hyperautomation
elements.def: When an organisation tries to hand as many of its everyday tasks as possible to computers, using several kinds of software and AI together.
elements.talk: If a business automated everything it could, what should it still keep people doing?
elements.picture_alt: An invoice passes through three kinds of automation. AI reads the amount, rules match it to an order, and payment software schedules payment. People review exceptions.

elements.name: Workflow Orchestration
elements.def: Planning and running the order of steps in a whole process, across different apps and people, such as getting a new pupil’s details from the form to the register. Contrast with Orchestrator.
elements.talk: Map how a lost-property report travels around your school. Where could automation help, and where would a person be better?
elements.picture_alt: A lost-coat report moves in order between the pupil, the school office and an app: report, log it, find, email, collect.

elements.name: Trigger
elements.def: The event that starts an automation — a new email, a form submission, a scheduled time.
elements.talk: Design a helpful automation: “When this happens, do that.” What could make it go wrong?
elements.picture_alt: Sending a form triggers a system to log it. A new email and a scheduled time are two other possible triggers.

elements.name: Event-Driven Automation
elements.def: Automations that start as soon as something happens in another app, such as a new booking, instead of waiting for a set time. Triggers and webhooks are how this usually works.
elements.talk: Should an app act the instant something happens, or wait for a person to check first? When?
elements.picture_alt: When a parcel arrives at 2 pm, the event-driven app reacts straight away while the scheduled one waits until 6 pm.

elements.name: API Integration
elements.def: Connecting apps so they pass information and actions to each other automatically, through their APIs: the doors one program opens for another.
elements.talk: Which of your information would you be happy for apps to share automatically, and which not?
elements.picture_alt: A homework app passes a Friday due date through a doorway to a calendar app, which sends back a message that it was added.

elements.name: Webhook
elements.def: A message one app sends to another the moment something happens — often used to kick off a workflow.
elements.talk: An app sends a message the moment you do something. What information might it be sharing?
elements.picture_alt: The moment a payment is made in a shop app, a message flies to the delivery app, which starts packing the order.

elements.name: Low-Code / No-Code
elements.def: Building apps and automations with visual, drag-and-drop tools and little or no hand-written code.
elements.talk: If anyone can build an app without coding, who makes sure it is safe and fair?
elements.picture_alt: Someone builds an automation without code by dragging an Email block into place under Form and If blocks.

elements.name: Intelligent Document Processing
elements.def: Using AI to read in documents such as forms, letters and invoices, sort them by type and pull out key details like names and dates (IDP).
elements.talk: An AI reads and sorts school forms. What could go wrong if it misreads one?
elements.picture_alt: AI reads an invoice, labels it as an invoice and pulls out who it is from, the date and the total of £120.

elements.name: Optical Character Recognition
elements.def: Converting images of text, such as scans or photos, into machine-readable text (OCR).
elements.talk: Try reading messy handwriting. Why might a computer find it hard, and whose handwriting might it struggle with most?
elements.picture_alt: A photo of the handwritten word Hello is read letter by letter into typed text, with the computer unsure whether one letter is an l or a 1.

elements.name: Process Mining
elements.def: Using the records computers keep to see how work really gets done, where it slows down, and which steps could be automated.
elements.talk: If software watches how work really gets done, how could that help people, and how could it feel like being watched?
elements.picture_alt: Computer records are turned into a map of how work really flows, showing ordering to checking takes 2 minutes but checking to paying takes 3 days.

elements.name: Business Rules Engine
elements.def: Software that follows a list of ‘if this, then that’ rules written by people, so the same case always gets the same decision, such as ‘if a book is 7 days late, send a reminder’.
elements.talk: Write three if-then rules for a school canteen. Which cases would your rules get wrong?
elements.picture_alt: Canteen orders pass through if-then rules, so the pasta always gets yes and the nut bar always gets no.

elements.name: Straight-Through Processing
elements.def: When a computer handles a whole job, such as a payment or an order, from start to finish without a person checking it.
elements.talk: Should any decision about a person go from start to finish with no one checking it? Which ones?
elements.picture_alt: An order moves along a conveyor from ordered to paid to sent, all by computer, with an empty space where a person would check.

elements.name: Digital Worker
elements.def: A marketing name for a software bot or AI agent set up to do a fixed set of tasks, described by its sellers as if it were a member of staff.
elements.talk: Should a software bot be called a “worker”? What does that word suggest?
elements.picture_alt: A team chart with three people, Payroll, Budgets and Manager, and a bot with its own job title, Invoices.

elements.name: Chatbot
elements.def: A program that people can chat with by typing or speaking, from simple scripted helpers to AI assistants that produce replies from patterns in text. If a chatbot ever encourages you to hurt yourself or keep secrets, stop and tell a trusted adult, or call Childline free on 0800 1111.
elements.talk: How is talking to a chatbot different from talking to a friend or a teacher?
elements.teacher_note: Pupils can also contact Samaritans free on 116 123, any time.

elements.name: Virtual Assistant
elements.def: A voice or chat assistant, such as the one on a phone or smart speaker, that carries out tasks like setting reminders or searching. Contrast with Chatbot (mainly conversation) and Copilot (built into one app).
elements.talk: What should a virtual assistant be allowed to remember about you?
elements.picture_alt: A pupil asks a chat assistant to move their club to Tuesday, and the assistant moves it in the calendar.

elements.name: Copilot
elements.def: An AI assistant built into an app or workflow that works alongside you — suggesting and drafting rather than acting alone.
elements.talk: Is work done with a copilot still your own work? Where would you draw the line?
elements.picture_alt: A pupil writes a sentence while an AI beside them suggests the next words in grey, and the pupil chooses to accept or edit.

elements.name: Responsible AI
elements.def: Developing and using AI in ways that are safe, fair, transparent and accountable.
elements.talk: Write three rules for using AI responsibly in your school.
elements.picture_alt: An AI must pass a checklist before it is used, with Safe, Fair, Transparent and Accountable all ticked, and a person linked to Accountable as the one in charge.

elements.name: AI Ethics
elements.def: Thinking about what is right and wrong in how people build and use AI, from asking permission to use someone’s data to its effects on jobs and society. Contrast with Responsible AI, which puts these ideas into practice.
elements.talk: Who should decide what is right and wrong for AI: the companies, governments or the public?
elements.picture_alt: Under the heading 'We can build it. But should we?', a signpost points to Consent, Any harm and Society, while a person and an AI stand at the post.

elements.name: Bias
elements.def: When an AI keeps treating some groups of people unfairly, often because the data it learned from was unbalanced.
elements.talk: Where could bias in an AI cause real harm, for example in jobs, policing or exam results?
elements.picture_alt: Training data shows thirteen people of one kind and only one of another, so the AI says yes to the first kind and no to the second.

elements.name: Fairness
elements.def: Making sure an AI system’s outcomes don’t unjustly favour or disadvantage particular people or groups.
elements.talk: Is it fair if an AI is right 95% of the time, but is wrong most often for one group?
elements.picture_alt: On the same task, the system gets nine of ten answers right for Group A and six of ten for Group B. The gap prompts a fairness investigation.

elements.name: Explainability
elements.def: Ways of showing people why an AI system gave a particular answer or decision, such as which information mattered most (XAI, explainable AI). Contrast with Transparency and Mechanistic Interpretability.
elements.talk: Which decisions about you would you want explained, and who should do the explaining?
elements.picture_alt: An AI gives an essay grade of C and, asked why, shows bars for what lowered it, too short and spelling, and what raised it, good ideas.

elements.name: Transparency
elements.def: Being open about when AI is being used, how it works and what data it relies on.
elements.talk: When does it matter most to know you are talking to an AI, and when might it not matter?
elements.picture_alt: A chatbot says 'I'm an AI', above a label that lists AI used: yes, how it works: predicts words, and data: public web.

elements.name: Alignment
elements.def: Research and testing that tries to make an AI system’s behaviour match what people intend and value, for example not taking shortcuts that meet the instruction but miss its point.
elements.talk: How would you check that an AI is really doing what people want, not just what they asked?
elements.picture_alt: A person asks an AI for top marks, and the AI aims at the target of really learning rather than the faded shortcut of copying.

elements.name: Guardrails
elements.def: Rules and filters that keep an AI system’s inputs and outputs within safe, acceptable bounds.
elements.talk: Should a chatbot for young people have stricter rules than one for adults? Which rules?
elements.picture_alt: Rails on either side of an AI let a homework question in and a helpful answer out, while an unsafe request and a harmful reply are blocked outside them.

elements.name: Human-in-the-Loop
elements.def: Keeping a person involved to review, approve or correct AI decisions before they take effect.
elements.talk: Where should a person always have the final say, whatever the AI suggests?
elements.picture_alt: An AI suggests a mark of 4 out of 10, a teacher checks it and can approve it or send it back to change, and only after approval is the mark sent.

elements.name: Red Teaming
elements.def: Deliberately attacking or stress-testing an AI system to uncover vulnerabilities and harmful behaviour.
elements.talk: Why might a company pay people to try to break its own AI?
elements.picture_alt: Two testers fire trick prompts at an AI's shield to try to break it; two bounce off and one finds a weak spot to fix before launch.

elements.name: AI Safety
elements.def: Research and practice aimed at preventing AI systems from causing accidental or deliberate harm.
elements.talk: What is the biggest risk from AI in your life, and who should be working on it?
elements.picture_alt: Three layers of safety, tests, rules and checks, each have holes; an accident gets through the first layer and a misuse through two, but both are stopped.

elements.name: Privacy
elements.def: Keeping people's personal information safe and under their control, including data used to train or run AI. In the UK this is covered by the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018, updated by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
elements.talk: What would you never type into a chatbot? Why?
elements.picture_alt: Name, address and health details are locked away under UK GDPR, and only the homework question is sent on to the AI.

elements.name: Data Governance
elements.def: The policies that control how data is collected, stored, accessed and used across an organisation.
elements.talk: Who in your school decides how pupils' data is used? How would you find out?
elements.picture_alt: A policy book in the middle sets the rules as data moves through four steps: collect, store, access and use.

elements.name: AI Regulation
elements.def: Laws and standards that govern AI — such as the EU AI Act, which sets rules according to a system’s level of risk.
elements.talk: If you could add one law about AI, what would it be?
elements.picture_alt: A stepped pyramid of AI rules by risk level, from minimal risk at the bottom through limited and high risk to banned at the top, with an arrow showing more risk means more rules.

elements.name: Copyright & IP
elements.def: Questions over who owns AI training data and AI-generated content, and how creators’ rights are protected. In the UK, creators’ work is protected by the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
elements.talk: Should artists be asked, or paid, before their work is used to train an AI?
elements.picture_alt: An artist's copyrighted painting is fed into an AI, which makes a similar picture, while the artist asks to be asked first and a label asks who owns the new picture.

elements.name: AI Washing
elements.def: Exaggerating how much a product uses AI to ride the hype, such as labelling basic software “AI-powered”.
elements.talk: Find a product that says it is “AI-powered”. What does the AI actually do?
elements.picture_alt: A plain toaster wears a big AI-powered sticker, but a look inside shows it only has a timer that pops the toast after two minutes.

elements.name: Shadow AI
elements.def: Using AI tools at work or school that haven’t been approved, which can put private data at risk.
elements.talk: Why might staff or students use AI tools the school has not approved? What could go wrong?
elements.picture_alt: A pupil copies a list of pupil names from the school's approved apps into an app that has not been approved, with a warning sign for the private data.

elements.name: Human Premium
elements.def: The extra value people place on work, art and services verified as made by humans.
elements.talk: Would you pay more for art, music or writing you knew was made by a person? Why?
elements.picture_alt: Two almost identical pots sit on a shelf: the AI-made one costs £5 and the one checked as made by a person costs £40.

elements.name: AI Watermarking
elements.def: Signals, often invisible, added to AI-generated images, audio, video or text so tools can later check where they came from. Watermarks can sometimes be removed, so they are not proof on their own.
elements.talk: Should every AI-made image carry a watermark? Who would check?
elements.picture_alt: A detector finds an embedded watermark in a landscape image and reports “Mark detected”.

elements.name: AI Sovereignty
elements.def: A country’s or organisation’s ability to build, run and control its own AI, data and computing power, rather than relying on other countries or companies.
elements.talk: Should every country build its own AI, or share it? What are the risks either way?
elements.picture_alt: A country with its own flag holds its own computers, data and AI inside its border, under its own rules and control.

elements.name: Reverse Engineering
elements.def: Taking a finished product, program or AI model apart to work out how it was made and how it works.
elements.talk: Is taking something apart to see how it works always fair? When does it become copying?
elements.picture_alt: A finished robot toy is taken apart into gears, a chip and a battery, and a note works out how it runs: battery to chip to gears.

elements.name: Mechanistic Interpretability
elements.def: Looking inside an AI model, piece by piece, to find which parts of it store particular ideas and how they lead to its answers.
elements.talk: Why might it matter to understand what is happening inside an AI, not just what it says?
elements.picture_alt: In an illustrative test on the question “Capital of France?”, researchers mute a highlighted pathway. The model becomes less likely to answer Paris, evidence that the pathway contributes to its answer.

elements.name: Activation Steering
elements.def: Nudging a model’s internal signals while it responds, to strengthen or weaken a particular behaviour.
elements.talk: If people can nudge what an AI says from the inside, who should be allowed to do it?
elements.picture_alt: Inside a model, one control labelled kind is nudged upwards among several sliders, and the reply bubble says you've got this.

elements.name: Model Extraction
elements.def: Sending an AI system thousands of questions and using its answers to build a copy, without access to its files. It usually breaks the tool’s terms of use and may break the law.
elements.talk: Someone copies an AI by asking it thousands of questions. How is that like copying homework, and how is it different?
elements.picture_alt: Ten thousand questions go to a locked AI and its answers are used to build a dashed-outline copy of it, without opening its locked files.

elements.name: Refusal Direction
elements.def: A single pattern in a model’s internal numbers that researchers found is linked to it refusing unsafe requests. Removing this pattern can stop the model refusing, which is how abliteration works.
elements.talk: Why might researchers want to find the part of an AI model linked to refusing requests? How could that knowledge be used well or badly?
elements.picture_alt: An unsafe request enters the inside of a model and lines up with an arrow marked refusal direction, so the model replies sorry, I can't help.

elements.name: Abliteration
elements.def: Editing an AI model to strip out its safety protections, so it no longer refuses harmful requests. Doing this does not make harmful or illegal content legal.
elements.talk: Who should be responsible for keeping AI safe once a model is shared online?

elements.name: Uncensored Model
elements.def: A downloadable AI model that people have altered, by retraining or by abliteration, so it no longer refuses harmful requests. Illegal content is still illegal, whichever tool makes it. Contrast with jailbreaking, which tricks an unchanged model.
elements.talk: Who is responsible for what an AI makes: the person asking, the person who changed the tool, or both?

elements.name: Jailbreaking
elements.def: Writing prompts designed to trick an AI into ignoring its safety rules, without changing the model itself. It usually breaks the tool’s terms of use.
elements.talk: Why do AI tools have safety rules at all, and what could happen if anyone could switch them off?

elements.name: GPU
elements.def: Graphics Processing Unit: a chip first made for video games that can do thousands of calculations at the same time. That makes it the main chip used to train and run AI.
elements.talk: The chips that run AI are made by only a few companies. Why might that matter?
elements.picture_alt: A GPU chip packed with dozens of tiny cores, with many arrows going into it at once to show it does lots of sums at the same time.

elements.name: TPU & Accelerators
elements.def: Computer chips built just for AI. They do AI’s maths faster and use less power than ordinary chips. Google’s TPU (Tensor Processing Unit) is one example.
elements.talk: Why would a company design its own chips just for AI? What does that tell you about AI's cost?
elements.picture_alt: An ordinary chip beside a chip built for AI doing the same AI maths: the AI chip has a much longer speed bar and a much shorter power bar.

elements.name: Cloud AI
elements.def: AI that runs on powerful computers in big data centres and is used over the internet, rather than on your own device. Most chatbots work this way.
elements.talk: When you use an AI in the cloud, where does your data go? How could you find out?
elements.picture_alt: A phone, laptop and tablet connect over the internet to AI running on servers in a cloud, sending a question up and getting an answer back.

elements.name: Edge AI
elements.def: Running AI directly on devices such as phones, cameras or sensors, rather than in the cloud.
elements.talk: Is it safer for AI to run on your phone rather than in the cloud? What do you gain and lose?
elements.picture_alt: A phone uses its own AI chip to label a cat on its screen, with the link to the cloud crossed out to show nothing is uploaded.

elements.name: MLOps
elements.def: The work of keeping machine learning models working well once people are using them: updating, checking and fixing them.
elements.talk: An AI that worked well last year starts making mistakes. Why might that happen, and who should notice?
elements.picture_alt: Three snapshots of the same model over months of use: 95% accurate at launch, dropping to 70% with a warning, then back to 94% after it is updated.

elements.name: LLMOps
elements.def: The everyday work of running large language model tools well: keeping track of prompts, testing the answers, watching the costs and spotting harmful output.
elements.talk: How would you check that a school chatbot is still giving safe answers every week?
elements.picture_alt: A chatbot in the middle of a weekly loop of four checks: prompts, tests, costs and safety.

elements.name: Vector Database
elements.def: A database that stores information as lists of numbers (embeddings), so it can quickly find things with a similar meaning. Many chatbots use one to look things up before they answer.
elements.talk: If an AI looks up answers in a database, what happens when the database is out of date?
elements.picture_alt: The word puppy is turned into a list of numbers and matched against a database of stored words, where dog is marked as the closest match ahead of kitten and bus.

elements.name: Model Serving
elements.def: The computers and software that run a trained model and answer requests from many people at once.
elements.talk: What happens to an app when millions of people ask it questions at once?
elements.picture_alt: Four people send questions to a tall rack of servers running one AI model and each gets an answer back, with millions more like them.

elements.name: Quantisation
elements.def: Shrinking an AI model by storing its numbers with fewer digits, a bit like rounding 3.14159 to 3.1. The model gets smaller, faster and cheaper to run, but can become slightly less accurate.
elements.talk: Would you choose a smaller, faster AI on your phone or a bigger one in the cloud? Why?
elements.picture_alt: A rounded weight illustrates lower precision. An example model uses 4 GB for its weights instead of 16 GB.

elements.name: Distillation
elements.def: Training a smaller “student” model to mimic the behaviour of a larger “teacher” model.
elements.talk: A small model is trained to copy a big one’s answers. What mistakes or biases might be copied across too?
elements.picture_alt: For the same unfinished sentence, a teacher model favours butter over jam and salt. A smaller student learns a similar pattern of predictions.

elements.name: Open-Weight Model
elements.def: A model whose trained parameters are publicly released, so anyone can run, study or adapt it, usually under a licence that sets some rules. Sharing it openly helps research, but also lets people remove its safety features.
elements.talk: Should powerful AI models be free for anyone to download and change? Argue both sides.
elements.picture_alt: An unlocked file of model weights with arrows to three people who run, study and adapt it, and a cracked shield warning that safety can be removed.

elements.name: Small Language Model
elements.def: A compact language model designed to run quickly and cheaply, often directly on a device.
elements.talk: A small AI model is quicker and cheaper to run but usually makes more mistakes. For which school tasks would a small model be good enough?
elements.picture_alt: A small model answers in one second on a laptop, beside a large model that needs a whole room of server racks.

elements.name: Evals
elements.def: Structured tests that measure a model’s accuracy, safety and behaviour on specific tasks.
elements.talk: How would you test an AI homework helper before letting a class use it?
elements.picture_alt: A test results sheet for an AI showing scores for accuracy (46 out of 50), safety (50 out of 50) and behaviour (31 out of 50).

elements.name: Scaling Laws
elements.def: The pattern researchers have seen that AI models tend to get better, in a predictable way, when they are made bigger and trained on more data with more computing power.
elements.talk: If bigger AI keeps getting better, should we keep building bigger? What are the costs?
elements.picture_alt: In an illustrative series of training runs, prediction error drops steeply at first, then more slowly as compute increases. A dashed extension and an open circle show a forecast.

elements.name: Data Pipeline
elements.def: The automated flow that collects, cleans and prepares data for training and analysis.
elements.talk: Data is collected, cleaned and fed to AI. At which step could mistakes or bias creep in?
elements.picture_alt: Data from several files is collected in a jumble, cleaned by throwing out a bad item, and prepared in neat rows that feed into training an AI.
